decks.title: Members of a Class, Abstraction and Objects
goals: Identify data members, member methods, local variables and parameters in a class
Explain how member methods read, change and return the state of an object
Model a real-life entity as a class by choosing its attributes for a purpose (abstraction)
Create several objects from one class with new and use them with the dot operator

slides.heading: Class as the basis of all computation
slides.body_md: Part 1: the **members of a class**, three kinds of variable, **abstraction**, the class as an **object factory**, and **new**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: members of a class, the three kinds of variable, methods that change state and return values, abstraction, the class as an object factory, and new with the dot operator
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome. In Java every program is built from classes. In this part we look inside a class: its data members and member methods, and the difference between data members, local variables and parameters. Then we model real things as classes, choosing only the attributes that matter, and see how one class makes many objects with the new operator.

slides.heading: Entities, state and behaviour
slides.body_md: A real-life **entity** is modelled by a class. Its **attributes** become **data members** (the state) and what it can do becomes **member methods** (the behaviour).

rows: can be issued a number, recharged, used, checked

visual.alt: Table that maps a real metro card to the class SmartCard: its number, money and journeys become the data members cardNo, balance and trips; what it can do becomes the member methods setCard, recharge, travel and show
visual.caption: Attributes become data members; actions become member methods.

slides.narration: Think of a metro smart card. It has a number, some money, and a count of journeys. These attributes become the data members of the class: the state of the card. The card can be issued a number, recharged, used for a journey and checked. These actions become member methods: the behaviour. State and behaviour together make an object.

The member methods section lists setCard, recharge, travel and show, with a note that bonus is a local variable of recharge and no, amount and fare are parameters
visual.caption: Anatomy of a class: data members on one side, member methods on the other.

slides.narration: This is the anatomy of the class SmartCard. The data members are written once, outside every method: card number, balance and trips. Then come the member methods, each with a return type, a name and a list of parameters in brackets. Inside the method recharge there is also a local variable called bonus. Every object made from the class gets its own copy of the data members.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: identify the members
slides.body_md: Look at the class above. For every name, find **where it is declared**; that tells its kind. The methods are setCard, recharge, travel and show.

visual.alt: Table that classifies each name of the class SmartCard: cardNo, balance and trips are data members; no, amount and fare are parameters; bonus is a local variable of recharge
visual.caption: Where a name is declared tells you what kind of variable it is.

slides.narration: Let us sort the names of the class SmartCard. Card number, balance and trips are declared in the class outside every method, so they are data members. The names no, amount and fare are written in method headings, so they are parameters. The name bonus is declared inside the body of recharge, so it is a local variable. The class has three data members and four member methods.

slides.heading: Data member, parameter, local variable
slides.body_md: The three kinds of variable differ in **where they are declared**, **how long they live** and whether they get a **default value**.

rows: yes (`0 / 0.0 / false / null / null` for Plot)
takes the value of the argument
none: variable total might not have been initialized

visual.alt: Table comparing data members, parameters and local variables by place of declaration, creation, life and default value; a local variable has no default and javac says variable total might not have been initialized
visual.caption: Only data members get default values.

slides.narration: The three kinds of variable differ in three ways. A data member is declared in the class, is created with the object and has a default value. A parameter is declared in the method heading and takes the value of the argument. A local variable is declared inside the method, starts afresh at each call and has no default value. Using it before giving it a value is a compile time error.

slides.body_md: Choose the correct answer.
slides.narration: Look for the variable declared inside the body of a method.

slides.heading: Methods that read and change state
slides.body_md: A member method can **read** the data members, **change** them with assignment, or both. A change made by one call is still there at the next call.

headers: What it does to the state
rows: changes balance (adds the amount and any bonus)
changes balance and trips, but only when the fare can be paid
only reads the data members and prints them

visual.alt: Table of the four member methods of SmartCard: setCard assigns cardNo, recharge changes balance, travel changes balance and trips only when the fare can be paid, and show only reads; the return types are void, void, boolean and void

slides.narration: Member methods work on the data members. The method set card assigns the number. Recharge changes the balance. Travel changes the balance and the trips, but only when the fare can be paid. Show only reads the data members and prints them. A change made by one call stays in the object, and the next call sees it.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: tracing the state of one card

visual.alt: Trace table of the state of one SmartCard object: after new SmartCard() it shows Card 0: balance 0.0, trips 0; after c.setCard(4501); it shows Card 4501: balance 0.0, trips 0; after c.recharge(500); it shows Card 4501: balance 525.0, trips 0; after c.travel(35.5); it shows Card 4501: balance 489.5, trips 1; after c.travel(900); it shows Card 4501: balance 489.5, trips 1
visual.caption: The last call is refused: the balance and trips do not change.

slides.narration: Let us follow one card. A new card has everything at zero. Then the number is set. Recharging with five hundred earns the bonus of twenty five, so the balance is five hundred twenty five. A journey of thirty five and a half leaves four hundred eighty nine and a half, with one trip. The last journey costs nine hundred, which the balance cannot pay, so nothing changes.

slides.heading: Methods that return values
slides.body_md: The **return type** in the heading says what comes back. A **void** method returns nothing. Any other method must end with **return** and a value of that type.

rows: nothing: it cannot be stored in a variable

visual.alt: Table of values returned by member methods: travel returns true when the fare is paid and false when it is refused, average returns a double, and show returns nothing
visual.caption: A void method returns nothing; any other method must return a value of its declared type.

slides.narration: The return type in the method heading says what kind of value comes back. Travel is a boolean method. It returns true when the fare is paid and false when it is refused, so the caller can test it. Average returns a double. Show is void: it returns nothing, so its call cannot be stored in a variable.

slides.heading: Abstraction: choose what matters
slides.body_md: **Abstraction** means modelling only the attributes and actions that the program **needs**. A different purpose gives a different class for the same entity.

rows: a metro smart card in the fare program
colour of the card, photo of the holder, thickness
printing the card, cutting it into pieces

visual.alt: Table of abstraction for a metro smart card: the class keeps cardNo, balance and trips with the actions recharge, travel and show, and leaves out the colour, the photo and the thickness
visual.caption: Abstraction keeps only what the program needs.

slides.narration: No class can describe everything about a real thing. Abstraction means keeping only what the program needs. For a fare program a metro card needs a number, a balance and a trip count, and the actions recharge, travel and show. The colour of the card or the photo of the holder would only add clutter. A different program, such as an identity check, would choose different attributes.

slides.body_md: A class is a **blueprint**, and also an **object factory**: each use of **new** makes one more **object** with its own copy of the data members.

nodes.label: object made, members get default values

visual.alt: Flow of creating an object: the variable p is declared, new SeedPacket creates the object with default values, its reference is stored in p, and p is then used with the dot operator to call set and show
visual.caption: Declaring a variable and creating an object are two different things.

slides.narration: Two things happen in one statement. The part before the equals sign declares a reference variable named p. The new operator makes the object, giving its data members default values, and returns its reference, which is stored in p. After that, p is used with the dot operator to call the methods of the object.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a class for a real-life entity

visual.alt: Table of results for two SeedPacket objects created from one class: a shows Tomato: 50 seeds, Rs 25.0 and b shows Marigold: 120 seeds, Rs 30.0; the cost per seed is 0.5 for a and 0.25 for b
visual.caption: The same method gives different answers on different objects.

slides.narration: Here is a class written for a seed packet: three data members and methods to set, price and show. In main, two objects are made. The first is a tomato packet of fifty seeds for twenty five rupees, which costs half a rupee a seed. The second is a marigold packet of one hundred twenty seeds for thirty rupees, which costs a quarter of a rupee. One method, two answers.

slides.heading: Message passing with the dot operator
slides.body_md: **object.method(arguments)** sends a message to the object before the dot. The method works on **that object's** data members. An object can also be passed **as an argument**.

rows: a, and b is passed in
b, and a is passed in

visual.alt: Table of four calls with the dot operator on two seed packets: a.costPerSeed() gives 0.5; b.costPerSeed() gives 0.25; a.cheaperThan(b) gives false; b.cheaperThan(a) gives true
visual.caption: object.method(): the object before the dot receives the message.

slides.narration: The dot operator sends a message to an object. The cost per seed call on a uses the data of a. The same call on b uses the data of b. The method cheaper than receives another packet as its argument and compares its cost with the cost of the object that received the message. A tomato packet is not cheaper than a marigold packet, but the marigold is cheaper than the tomato.

slides.narration: A hostel room has four beds. The method admit takes only as many students as there are free beds, changes the data member occupied, and returns the number admitted. Asking for three and then three admits three, then only one, and leaves no vacancy. Asking for five and then one admits four, then none. Always read the returned value, not the request.

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: data members, member methods, local variables and parameters, abstraction, the class as an object factory and the dot operator

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Data members hold the state, and each object has its own copy with default values. Member methods give the behaviour and can read, change or return values. Local variables and parameters live only for one call. Abstraction keeps just the attributes the program needs. A class is an object factory: new makes objects, and the dot operator sends them messages.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: To classify a name, find where it is declared: in the class (data member), in the heading (parameter) or in the body (local variable).
A local variable starts afresh at every call; a data member keeps its value as long as the object lives.
Declaring `SeedPacket p;` creates no object; `new` does. Count the `new`s to count the objects.
Trace each object separately: a call on one object never changes another.
In a program, give values with an `accept` or `set` method, create the object with `new` in `main`, and call the methods with the dot operator.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. To classify a name, find where it is declared. Remember that a local variable starts afresh at each call, while a data member keeps its value. A declaration alone creates no object, so count the uses of new. Trace every object separately. In a program, give values with an accept method, create the object in main, and call its methods with the dot operator.

goals: Distinguish primitive data types from composite (class) types with examples
Explain what a variable holds: a value for a primitive, a reference for an object
Predict default values, copies, == comparisons and NullPointerException
Pass objects to methods and return objects from methods

slides.heading: Primitive and composite types
slides.body_md: Part 2: **primitive** and **composite** types, **value** and **reference**, default values, copying, **==**, **null** and **String**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: primitive and composite types, declaring variables, value and reference, default values, copying, comparing with double equals and null, and objects as arguments and results
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part. Every variable has a data type. We compare primitive types, which hold a value, with composite types made from classes, which hold a reference to an object. We study declarations, default values, what copying really copies, why double equals can surprise us, what null means, and how objects travel into and out of methods.

slides.heading: Two families of data types
slides.body_md: **Primitive** types are built into Java and hold a simple value. **Composite** (class or reference) types are defined by a **class** and group members together.

rows: a class (built in or written by you)

visual.alt: Comparison table of primitive and composite types: examples, who defines them, what a variable holds, memory size and the default value as a data member

slides.narration: Java has two families of data types. The primitive types, such as int, double, char and boolean, are built into the language. A variable of a primitive type holds the value itself. A composite type is defined by a class, whether a library class like String or one you write. A variable of that type holds a reference to an object, and the size of the object depends on its members.

slides.heading: Primitive types have a fixed size
slides.body_md: The size of each primitive type is **fixed by the language**: an int is always 4 bytes, a double always 8, in every program.

visual.alt: Table of the fixed sizes of six primitive types in bytes: byte 1, short 2, char 2, int 4, long 8, double 8
visual.caption: The size of a primitive type never changes from one program to another.

slides.narration: The size of a primitive type never changes. A byte takes one byte, a short and a char take two, an int takes four, and a long and a double take eight. The numbers in the table were printed by Java itself. An object is different: it must hold all the data members of its class, so its size depends on the class.

slides.heading: Default values by type
slides.body_md: Data members get a default value: **0** for int, **0.0** for double, **false** for boolean and **null** for every class type. A **local variable** gets **no** default.

slides.narration: The rule is simple. Numeric data members start at zero of their type, a boolean starts false, and every member of a class type starts as null. This applies only to data members. A local variable has no default value, and reading it before assigning a value is rejected by the compiler.

slides.narration: When an object variable is copied, only the reference is copied, not the object. After b gets the value of a, there is still one packet, with two names. A change made through b is seen through a, because both lead to the same object. To get a second object, we must use new again.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: value copy against reference copy

visual.alt: Trace table: copying an int leaves x at 5 when y changes; before b.set, a shows Tomato: 50 seeds, Rs 25.0; after b.set, a shows Okra: 30 seeds, Rs 18.0 because a and b refer to one object

slides.narration: Let us trace both copies together. The int y changes to nine, and x stays five. For the packets, b is a copy of a, so they share one object. Calling set through b changes the packet to Okra, thirty seeds, eighteen rupees, and now a shows Okra as well. The output is five and nine on one line, and the Okra packet on the next.

slides.body_md: Write the exact output.
slides.narration: Remember which copy shares one object and which copy keeps separate values.

slides.heading: Comparing with ==
slides.body_md: For primitives, **==** compares **values**. For objects, **==** compares **references**: it is true only when both variables refer to the **same object**.

rows: c holds the same reference as a

visual.alt: Table of equality tests on SeedPacket objects: a == b is false, a.price == b.price is true, a == c is true
visual.caption: For objects, == compares references, not contents.

slides.narration: The double equals operator compares what the variables hold. For two prices, which are doubles, it compares the numbers. For two object variables, it compares the references. The packets a and b were made by separate uses of new, so a double equals b is false even though their data are equal. The variable c is a copy of a, so a double equals c is true.

slides.heading: null and NullPointerException
slides.body_md: **null** is the value of a reference that refers to **no object**. Calling a method through it stops the program with a **NullPointerException**, a run-time error.

rows: run-time error: java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "SeedPacket.show()" because "this.packet" is null

visual.alt: Table about null: printing a null String shows null, while calling a method through a null reference stops the program with java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "SeedPacket.show()" because "this.packet" is null
visual.caption: null refers to no object, so there is nothing to receive the call.

slides.narration: Null means a reference that refers to no object. Printing a null String simply shows the word null. But calling a method through a null reference is a run time error: there is no object to receive the call. In the example, the shelf has never been given a packet, so its check method stops the program with a NullPointerException. The compiler cannot detect this in advance.

slides.heading: String: a built-in composite type
slides.body_md: **String** is a class of the Java library, so a String variable holds a **reference**, and it can be **null**. Its methods are called with the dot operator.

visual.alt: Table of String behaviour: a String variable called s holding Neem has length 4 and upper case NEEM; a String variable set to null prints null
visual.caption: String is a class, so a String variable holds a reference.

slides.narration: The type String is not primitive. It is a class of the Java library, so a String variable holds a reference to a String object. That is why we can call methods on it with the dot operator, such as length and to upper case. It is also why a String variable can be null. Strings are studied fully in a later chapter.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: objects as arguments

visual.alt: Table about arguments: cutObject receives a copy of the reference, so the price of the object becomes 20.0; cutNumber receives a copy of the value, so rate stays 25.0
visual.caption: Output of the program: 20.0 25.0

slides.narration: A method receives a copy of whatever argument is passed. For an object, the copy is a copy of the reference, so the method reaches the original object, and the price of the packet falls by five to twenty. For a double, the copy is a copy of the value, so only the parameter changes, and the variable in main stays twenty five. The output is twenty point zero and twenty five point zero.

slides.heading: Objects returned from methods
slides.body_md: A method can **return an object**: the value that comes back is a **reference**. It may refer to an argument or to a **new** object made inside the method.

visual.alt: Table about a returned object: pick returns the reference of one of the arguments, so best.show() prints Marigold: 120 seeds, Rs 30.0 and best == b is true
visual.caption: A method can return a reference to an existing object.

slides.narration: A method can also return an object. What comes back is a reference. The pick method returns one of the two packets it received, not a copy. So the returned reference and the original variable lead to the same object, and double equals between them is true. A method may also create a new object with new and return that instead.

slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true.
slides.narration: Ask whether an assignment of an object variable copies the object or only the reference.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Primitive types hold a value and have a fixed size. Composite types come from classes; their variables hold a reference. A declaration alone creates no object. Copying an int copies the value, but copying an object variable copies the reference. Double equals on objects compares references. Null refers to no object, and calling a method through it gives a NullPointerException.

A method may be given **objects** as arguments and may **return an object**; both use references.

sections.body_md:
- **Copy:** `int y = x;` copies the value; `SeedPacket b = a;` copies the **reference**, so a and b are two names for one object (an alias): the copy program prints `5 9 / Okra: 30 seeds, Rs 18.0`.
- **Compare:** `==` on primitives compares values; on objects it compares references: for two packets with equal data `a == b` is false.
- **null:** a call through a null reference stops the program with a **NullPointerException** ("java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "SeedPacket.show()" because "this.packet" is null"); the compiler cannot see it.
- **Arguments:** an object argument passes a copy of the reference, so the method can change the object; a primitive argument passes a copy of the value, so the caller's variable does not change (`20.0 25.0`).
- **String** is a class: a String variable holds a reference and can be null.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Counting `SeedPacket c;` as an object: a declaration creates only a reference variable; only `new` creates an object.
- Expecting a local variable to keep its value between calls, or to have a default value.
- Thinking `b = a` for objects makes a copy of the object; it copies the reference.
- Using `==` to compare the contents of two objects.
- Calling a method through a variable that is still `null`.
- Storing the value of a `void` method in a variable.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Output questions: each line in the exact order and format.
- Error questions: the error named, with the line or the message.
- Programs (15 marks): the class (data members and methods), `main` with Scanner and `new`, the calls, the output, and the variable description or comments.
